title: Know your fabric, sew strong hand stitches, measure right

say: Know your fabric, sew strong hand stitches, and measure right.
This is the video for module one of Basic Tailoring and Garment Repair.
Almost every home has clothes waiting for small fixes. A home tailor earns from three kinds of work. Repair brings a damaged garment back to use.

say: Start with repair. It needs the least equipment and builds the habits you need later: straight stitching, neat finishing and pressing.

say: Before any job, check the fabric. Woven fabric is made from threads crossing at right angles, like a mat.
Ankara, shirting and denim are woven. They barely stretch, and their cut edges fray, so you must finish those edges.
Knit fabric is made from loops, like a sweater. T-shirts, jersey gowns and leggings are knits.
To test, pull gently. If it stretches easily and springs back, it is a knit. Knits need a stretchy stitch, such as a narrow zigzag, and a ballpoint needle.
Six hand stitches cover nearly every repair. Running stitch goes in and out in a straight line. Use it for tacking before machine sewing.

panel.heading: The right stitch for the job
items: Running stitch: basting and light seams
Backstitch: the strongest hand seam
Slip stitch: closes a gap invisibly
Blind hem: hems that must not show
Whipstitch: joins finished edges, patches
Overcast: stops a raw edge fraying

say: Backstitch is the strongest hand seam. Each stitch touches the last. Use it to mend split seams.

say: For example, Halima's neighbour brings a cotton blouse with a 6 cm split in the underarm seam. Only the stitching has broken.
Step one. Halima turns the blouse inside out and pulls out the loose broken threads.

panel.heading: Mending a split underarm seam
items: Turn inside out, pull out broken threads
Pin edges along the old stitching line
Knot 1 cm before the split
Backstitch to 1 cm past the split
Two locking stitches, trim, press

say: Step two. She pins the two edges together along the original stitching line. She can still see it as small holes.

panel.heading: Mending a split underarm seam
items: Turn inside out, pull out broken threads
Pin edges along the old stitching line
Knot 1 cm before the split
Backstitch to 1 cm past the split
Two locking stitches, trim, press

say: Step three. She starts with a knot about 1 cm before the split, in old stitching that is still good.

panel.heading: Mending a split underarm seam
items: Turn inside out, pull out broken threads
Pin edges along the old stitching line
Knot 1 cm before the split
Backstitch to 1 cm past the split
Two locking stitches, trim, press

say: Step four. She sews backstitch, with stitches about 2 to 3 mm long, and ends 1 cm past the split.

panel.heading: Mending a split underarm seam
items: Turn inside out, pull out broken threads
Pin edges along the old stitching line
Knot 1 cm before the split
Backstitch to 1 cm past the split
Two locking stitches, trim, press

say: Step five. She finishes with two locking stitches, trims the thread, and presses the seam.
Never end by simply cutting the thread. The stitches will pull out in the first wash. And do not pull stitches too tight, or the fabric will pucker.

Two locking stitches, trim, press
panel.rule: Overlap into good stitching and always lock the end

say: For example, Bisi brings her son's school trousers to Fatima. He wears them with his school shoes, and Fatima folds the hem up until it just touches the top of the shoe.

panel.heading: Shortening school trousers
items: Fold up to touch the top of the shoe
Measure: 6 cm too long
Old hem 3 cm, so 9 cm below the fold
Keep a 4 cm hem allowance
Trim off 5 cm

say: She pins and measures. The trousers are 6 cm too long.

panel.heading: Shortening school trousers
items: Fold up to touch the top of the shoe
Measure: 6 cm too long
Old hem 3 cm, so 9 cm below the fold
Keep a 4 cm hem allowance
Trim off 5 cm

say: The old hem is 3 cm deep. So there is 9 cm of fabric below the new fold.

items: Fold up to touch the top of the shoe

Keep a 4 cm hem allowance
Trim off 5 cm

say: Trousers usually need a hem allowance of about 4 cm. She marks the fold line with chalk, then a cutting line 4 cm below it.

say: So she keeps 4 cm and trims off 5 cm. Fabric cut too short cannot be put back, so measure both legs before cutting.

say: Now set up a safe corner, with good light by day and a bright bulb at night.
Keep pins and needles in a closed tin, never in your mouth, and keep scissors closed and away from children.
Stand the iron on its heel, keep its cable away from the edge, and switch it off at the wall when you finish.
Run any generator outside, away from doors and windows. Its fumes contain carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas you cannot smell.

panel.heading: A safe, well-lit work corner
items: Good light on your work
Needles and pins in a closed box
Scissors closed, out of children's reach
Iron unplugged after use
No trailing cables
Generator outside, away from windows

say: So remember. Start with repairs. Check woven or knit. Backstitch is the strongest hand seam, and every line ends with locking stitches.
Measure snug but not tight, write numbers in centimetres at once, and mark both lines before you cut.

panel.heading: Key points
items: Start with repair work
Woven frays; knit stretches and curls
Backstitch is strongest; finish with locks
Measure snug, write in cm at once
Mark fold line and cutting line first

say: Your practice tasks: sort six fabric scraps into woven and knit, sew a sampler with all six stitches, measure one family member, and set up your safe work corner.
Now continue with the lessons below.
